prime.problem: You've written get_stats, merge, a training loop, encode and decode, but only as separate pieces, and your ids mean nothing to GPT-4. A model trained on GPT-4's ids can only read ids produced by exactly GPT-4's tokenizer, and tiktoken gives you that tokenizer without showing how it's built.
prime.fits: This is the capstone of the byte pair encoding and real-tokenizer cards. It combines the training loop and encode with the regex pre-split and special tokens, and checks the result against tiktoken id for id. The sentencepiece card comes next.
expect: special tokens split off before BPE
prime.goal: Build a tokenizer whose ids match tiktoken's cl100k_base, and explain what each of its four layers (regex, merges, byte order, special tokens) contributes and what breaks without it.

attend: Why does the regex tokenizer compress less than the basic one on the same text, and why is that still the better tokenizer?
tiktoken stores only bytes → rank. What property of BPE lets you rebuild the pair behind every rank?
Why does the replay for a token have to stop before reaching the token's own rank?
What goes wrong if you load GPT-4's merges but feed them raw byte values, and why do most merges then never fire?
Why must special tokens be cut out before the regex runs, and why does tiktoken refuse them by default?

must: Regex pre-split → merges can't cross letters/digits/punctuation/space → the tokenizer spends its merges on words instead of e␣ or citation boilerplate → worse raw compression (2.13× vs 2.36× on taylorswift.txt) but more meaningful tokens

A token's rank is also its place in the merge order → replaying BPE on its bytes with only lower-ranked merges ends exactly at its two parents → the whole 100,000-merge table can be rebuilt from bytes → rank alone

Merges are keyed by token ids, and GPT-4's byte tokens are permuted (h is 71, not 104) → encoding raw bytes looks up the wrong pairs → most merges never fire (41 ids instead of 14) → you must shuffle bytes on encode and un-shuffle on decode
Same algorithm + same merges + same regex + same byte order + same special-token handling → identical ids → any one layer wrong silently gives different ids that GPT-4's embedding table would misread
elevated: Special tokens are split off with re.split and a capturing group before the regex → their ids never pass through BPE → and because typed text could contain <|endoftext|>, tiktoken raises unless you pass allowed_special
reference: the exact GPT4_SPLIT_PATTERN string (copy it from regex.py)
enc._mergeable_ranks (a private tiktoken attribute) and its 100,256 entries
the byte_shuffle values (a → 64, space → 220, byte 0 → 188) and that they follow GPT-2's bytes_to_unicode order

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the encode path of the finished GPT-4 tokenizer for "<|endoftext|>hello world", labelling which of the four exercise steps each box comes from. Then write 3–4 sentences on the two hurdles in step 3.
checklist: special tokens are cut out first and go straight to their ids
the ordinary text is split by the GPT-4 regex, and each chunk is encoded separately
each chunk's bytes go through byte_shuffle before merging
merges are applied lowest rank first until none applies (the encode card's loop)
hurdle 1: tiktoken stores ranks, not pairs; replay BPE below each rank to recover the pair
hurdle 2: single bytes are permuted, so shuffle on encode and un-shuffle on decode

retrieve.q: Explain why a tokenizer that compresses taylorswift.txt better (2.36×) is still the one Karpathy moves away from in step 2.
answer: the basic tokenizer's merges cross categories: 110 of 256 glue words to spaces or punctuation
that wastes vocabulary on things like e␣ and a 32-byte citation phrase
the regex version's tokens are whole words and pieces of words, which generalise better across texts

retrieve.q: Walk through recovering the parent pair of b'hello' (rank 15339) from _mergeable_ranks.
answer: start from single bytes h e l l o
repeatedly merge the adjacent pair with the lowest rank, but only ranks below 15339
h e l l o → h el l o → h el lo → h ello, then stop
the two remaining parts are the parents: (71, 4896) → 15339

retrieve.q: Walk through what encode does to the chunk hello, from string to id, including the byte shuffle.
answer: shuffle to 71 68 75 75 78
repeatedly merge the lowest-rank pair present in merges
ends as the single id 15339

retrieve.q: You need GPT-4-compatible ids in a production service. Choose between your minbpe-style GPT4Tokenizer and tiktoken, and say what the exercise version is still good for.
answer: tiktoken: the same ids, a Rust core, and it's the reference
your version: pure Python, far slower, and only checked on a few strings
your version (and minbpe) can train a vocabulary, which tiktoken can't
use the exercise to understand the layers, not to serve traffic

compare.q: Your GPT-4 tokenizer vs Llama 2's sentencepiece tokenizer: what unit does BPE run on in each, which design choice causes that, and how does each one fail on a character it rarely saw?
answer: GPT-4: BPE on UTF-8 bytes after a regex split, so every string is encodable from 256 byte tokens
sentencepiece: BPE on Unicode code points; rare code points fall back to byte tokens only if byte_fallback is on
GPT-4 fails soft: rare text just costs many tokens
sentencepiece without fallback fails hard: rare text becomes <unk>

compare.q: The train-loop card produces merges by counting; this card gets them from tiktoken. What's the same about the resulting merges dict, and what can't you learn from GPT-4's?
answer: both map (id, id) → new id, ordered by when the merge was made
both are used by the same encode loop, lowest rank first
GPT-4's comes without the pair counts or the training text, so you can only guess (e.g. from the leading space-run merges) what it was trained on

predict.q: Keep GPT-4's recovered merges and byte shuffle, but split with the GPT-2 regex instead. On "x = 1234567", will your ids still match tiktoken's? If not, where will they differ?
predict.answer: They differ, even though both give 6 tokens. GPT-2's regex keeps ␣1234567 as one chunk, while GPT-4's regex splits it into ␣, 123, 456, 7. GPT-4's merges never learned a space+digit token or anything longer than three digits, so BPE on the GPT-2 chunk ends as ␣ 123 45 67 ([220, 4513, 10961, 22] from tiktoken vs [220, 4513, 1774, 3080] from yours). On the lab's test string the two regexes happen to give identical chunks, so it would still match. That's why one test string isn't proof.

apply.task: By hand, recover the parent pair of b' world', whose rank is 1917. Start from the six single bytes and, at each step, merge the adjacent pair with the lowest rank below 1917 (look ranks up with enc._mergeable_ranks[...]). Then check your answer against the merges dict from the Build-it code.
apply.done: You reach [b' w', b'orld'] after four merges (or, ␣w, ld, orld), and merges[(289, 1410)] == 1917.
apply.hint: At each step, compute the rank of every adjacent pair (ranks.get(a + b)) and take the smallest one below 1917. When the only pair left is ␣w + orld, its rank is 1917 itself, so you stop.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that the regex tokenizer compresses less, or that the GPT-2 regex changes the ids?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the replay stops at the token's own rank, or why a byte permutation breaks nearly every merge?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: rank → merge order, or merge order → recoverable parents?
Which of the four layers would you check first if your ids differed from tiktoken on one string?
What will you look at again before the sentencepiece card?
